content: 4-Aminobutyrate aminotransferase (ABAT) is a protein encoded by the ABAT gene in humans. This gene is also known by other names, such as GABA, GABAT, 4-aminobutyrate transaminase, and NPD009. The ABAT gene is predominantly expressed in neuronal tissues. The enzyme 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase belongs to the group of pyridoxal 5-phosphate-dependent enzymes, which play a significant role in catalyzing reactions involving amino acids. ABAT is composed of two enzyme monomers, each with a molecular weight of 50 kDa. It has been identified that nearly one-third of human synapses contain GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid). GABA is a neurotransmitter with diverse roles in different regions of the central and peripheral nervous systems. It is also present in some non-neuronal tissues. The enzymes glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) and GABA aminotransferase (GABA-AT) are responsible for regulating GABA concentrations. A notable characteristic of GABA is its lack of fluorescence and electroactivity, which makes it challenging to measure enzymatic reactions involving GABA, as no peroxidase or dehydrogenase activity has been identified. Additionally, GABA has low lipophilicity, which hinders its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier. Researchers are actively investigating molecules with high lipophilicity to overcome this limitation. Quantifying GABA concentrations during cellular activity requires high spatial and temporal resolution. Historically, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was used to measure GABA levels. However, modern techniques now allow for the analysis and measurement of GABA in small volumes and over short time periods using electrochemiluminescence. GABA also functions as a trophic factor, influencing cellular activities such as rapid cell reproduction, cell death, and differentiation. Beyond the nervous system, GABA plays a role in intracellular communication. The enzyme 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase (ABAT) is crucial for the catabolism of GABA, an important inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. ABAT converts GABA into succinic semialdehyde. The active enzyme is a homodimer composed of 50-kDa subunits complexed with pyridoxal-5-phosphate. The protein sequence of ABAT shares over 95% similarity with its pig counterpart. GABA, as a trophic factor, affects cellular processes such as proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis. It also facilitates intracellular communication outside the nervous system. The production of the GABA-transaminase enzyme is regulated by the ABAT gene. ABAT's primary function is to prevent excessive brain activity by inhibiting the overloading of signals. It initiates the breakdown of GABA. Suppressing ABAT's activity has been explored as a potential treatment for conditions like gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). ABAT deficiency is a rare disorder. Symptoms of this deficiency have been observed in a Dutch family (two siblings) and a 6-month-old Japanese infant. Common clinical features include hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), hyperreflexia, developmental delays, psychomotor retardation, lethargy, refractory seizures, and abnormal EEG findings. Multiple alternatively spliced transcript variants encoding the same protein isoform have been identified for this gene. Uncontrolled GABA levels due to abnormal protein function can impact growth hormone regulation and overall development. A decrease in GABA concentration can lead to convulsions. The drug vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase, resulting in increased GABA levels in the brain. Recent studies have shown that elevated GABA levels can mitigate the effects of drug addiction. Suppression of ABAT, which increases GABA levels, has been linked to movement disabilities in children. The ABAT gene has also been implicated as a genetic cause of GERD. Furthermore, ABAT plays a critical role in mitochondrial nucleoside metabolism.
